title: Jurisdictional sift: Holdroyd and Musicians' Union
text:
SD/3/26-27
The Assistant Certification Officer’s Sift Decision under Section 108A of the
Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992
Susan Holdroyd Applicant
and
Musicians’ Union Respondent
Date of Decision 19 May 2026
1

Contents
Decision ............................................................................................................... 3
Background ......................................................................................................... 3
The relevant statutory provisions ..................................................................... 5
The relevant rules of the Union ......................................................................... 9
The Applicant’s submissions .......................................................................... 12
The Jurisdiction of the Certification Officer ................................................... 14
Conclusions ...................................................................................................... 20
2

Decision
1. Upon application by Susan Holdroyd (“the Applicant”) under section 108A of
the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992 (“the 1992
Act”):
I find that Susan Holdroyd’s application is not one which
the Certification Officer has the jurisdiction to
determine. Therefore, the application cannot be
accepted for determination by the Certification Officer
and is dismissed.
Background
2. Susan Holdroyd is known by the performing name Sue McCreeth. She is a
member of Musicians’ Union (“the Union” or “the Respondent”). She first
submitted an application for a declaration that there has been a breach of the
rules of the Respondent on 23 April 2026.
3. On the application form to the Certification Office, the complaint was
summarised as:
Complaint
I am lodging a formal complaint regarding a systemic
and procedural breach of Union Rules by the
Musicians' Union (MU) between 2018 and 2026. This
complaint concerns a fundamental failure to adhere to
the Union’s constitutional mandate and documented
procedural irregularities in the administration of the
Legal Assistance Scheme (LAS).
3

4. On 30 April 2026, the Certification Office wrote to the Applicant to inform her
that a preliminary view had been reached that the application did not fall
within the jurisdiction of the Certification Officer (CO).
5. The letter explained to the Applicant that the CO had delegated to me, as the
Assistant Certification Officer (ACO), responsibility for determining questions
of jurisdiction arising at the stage of initial consideration of applications.
6. Given the preliminary view that the application was outside the CO’s
jurisdiction, the Applicant was told that they had two options:
6.1. Option 1 was to withdraw the application, in which case no formal
decision would be made or issued and the matter would be closed;
Or,
6.2. Option 2 was to request that a formal decision be made following the
preliminary view. The Applicant was told that if they chose this option,
I would formally consider whether the application fell within the CO’s
jurisdiction and issue a written decision. That decision would be sent
to the Applicant, and the Union, and would be published on the CO’s
website.
7. The Applicant was also told that should they select option 2, they would then
have 2 weeks to provide any supplementary evidence or argument on which
they wished me to rely in determining the issue of jurisdiction.
8. On 8 May 2026, the Applicant confirmed their preference for a formal decision
regarding the issue of jurisdiction in respect of the first application.
9. The Applicant submitted a written submission, and an accompanying
document titled “SHORT VERSION PROCEDURAL MALICE”. While I have
not found it necessary to refer to specific extracts from the document, I have
carefully considered its contents in the course of making this jurisdictional sift
decision.
4

10. For the avoidance of any doubt, because the application has not been
accepted for determination by the CO for want of jurisdiction, there has been
no correspondence with the Respondent Union in respect of the application.
The relevant statutory provisions
11. The statutory provisions which are relevant for the purposes of this
application are as follows:
The Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidated)
Act 1992:
Right to apply to Certification Officer – s108A
(1) A person who claims that there has been a breach
or threatened breach of the rules of a trade union
relating to any of the matters mentioned in subsection
(2) may apply to the Certification Officer for a
declaration to that effect, subject to subsections (3) to
(7).
(2) The matters are—
(a) the appointment or election of a person to, or the
removal of a person from, any office;
(b) disciplinary proceedings by the union (including
expulsion);
(c) the balloting of members on any issue other than
industrial action;
(d) the constitution or proceedings of any executive
committee or of any decision-making meeting;
5

(e) such other matters as may be specified in an order
made by the Secretary of State.
(3) The applicant must be a member of the union or
have been one at the time of the alleged breach or
threatened breach.
(4) A person may not apply under subsection (1) in
relation to a claim if he is entitled to apply under section
80 in relation to the claim.
(5) No application may be made regarding—
(a) the dismissal of an employee of the union;
(b) disciplinary proceedings against an employee of the
union.
(6) An application must be made—
(a) within the period of six months starting with the day
on which the breach or threatened breach is alleged to
have taken place, or
(b) if within that period any internal complaints
procedure of the union is invoked to resolve the claim,
within the period of six months starting with the earlier
of the days specified in subsection (7).
(7) Those days are—
(a) the day on which the procedure is concluded, and
(b) the last day of the period of one year beginning with
the day on which the procedure is invoked.
6

(8) The reference in subsection (1) to the rules of a
union includes references to the rules of any branch or
section of the union.
(9) In subsection (2)(c) “industrial action” means a strike
or other industrial action by persons employed under
contracts of employment.
(10) For the purposes of subsection (2)(d) a committee
is an executive committee if—
(a) it is a committee of the union concerned and has
power to make executive decisions on behalf of the
union or on behalf of a constituent body,
(b) it is a committee of a major constituent body and has
power to make executive decisions on behalf of that
body, or
(c) it is a sub-committee of a committee falling within
paragraph (a) or (b).
(11) For the purposes of subsection (2)(d) a decision-
making meeting is—
(a) a meeting of members of the union concerned (or
the representatives of such members) which has power
to make a decision on any matter which, under the rules
of the union, is final as regards the union or which,
under the rules of the union or a constituent body, is
final as regards that body, or
(b) a meeting of members of a major constituent body
(or the representatives of such members) which has
power to make a decision on any matter which, under
7

the rules of the union or the body, is final as regards
that body.
(12) For the purposes of subsections (10) and (11), in
relation to the trade union concerned—
(a) a constituent body is any body which forms part of
the union, including a branch, group, section or region;
(b) a major constituent body is such a body which has
more than 1,000 members.
(13) Any order under subsection (2)(e) shall be made
by statutory instrument; and no such order shall be
made unless a draft of it has been laid before and
approved by resolution of each House of Parliament.
(14) If a person applies to the Certification Officer under
this section in relation to an alleged breach or
threatened breach he may not apply to the court in
relation to the breach or threatened breach; but nothing
in this subsection shall prevent such a person from
exercising any right to appeal against or challenge the
Certification Officer’s decision on the application to him.
(15) If—
(a) a person applies to the court in relation to an alleged
breach or threatened breach, and
(b) the breach or threatened breach is one in relation to
which he could have made an application to the
Certification Officer under this section,
8

he may not apply to the Certification Officer under this
section in relation to the breach or threatened breach.
254 The Certification Officer
(4) The Certification Officer may delegate to an
assistant certification officer such functions as he thinks
appropriate, and in particular may delegate to the
assistant certification officer for Scotland such functions
as he thinks appropriate in relation to organisations
whose principal office is in Scotland.
References to the Certification Officer in enactments
relating to his functions shall be construed accordingly.
The relevant rules of the Union
12. The Rules of the Union which are relevant for the purposes of this application
are as follows:
Rule II: Membership
1. Persons are eligible to join the MU if, at the time of
their application:
a. They are following the profession of music;
and,
b. They are not members of any other body of
musicians established for protective purposes
which has been proscribed by the EC; and,
c. They are not currently in a period of exclusion
following expulsion from MU membership and
9

have not been engaged in conduct contrary to
the Rules of the MU.
Such other persons may be admitted to membership as
may be deemed eligible by the EC.
2. Application for admission to the MU may be made by
such methods as the EC makes available, and shall be
sent together with the correct subscription.
3. Applications shall be granted or rejected under such
procedures and conditions as determined by the EC
and subject to conditions and/or payments of advance
subscriptions as determined by the EC.
4. If an application is rejected, the applicant may, within
a period of 21 days from the date the rejection is notified
to them, appeal to the EC to be reconsidered. Any
money paid by a rejected applicant to the MU shall be
refunded on completion of any unsuccessful appeal
against rejection.
5. A copy of the MU’s Rules will be supplied to any
person upon request either free of charge or on
payment of a reasonable charge.
6. Every member (except as provided for in sub-Rule 9
below) shall be attached to a Region, normally that in
which the member resides or performs the majority of
their professional activities. In the event of dispute
concerning the particular Region in which the member
shall be placed, the EC shall decide and this decision
shall be final.
10

7. The membership of any person who has previously
been a member of the MU shall date from their most
recent admission to the MU.
8. The membership of any person who makes a false
declaration in connection with their application for
membership may be declared void by the EC from the
beginning at its discretion and all sums paid by such
person to the MU forfeited.
9. The EC may appoint any person to be a member of
the MU on such conditions and for such period as the
EC decides. Save where the context otherwise requires
or admits, references in these Rules to a member or
members include all members of the MU.
10. Notwithstanding anything in these Rules the EC
may terminate the membership of any member if
necessary in order to comply with the decision of a
Disputes Committee of the Trades Union Congress.
11. A member may apply to resign from the MU and the
member’s resignation shall be accepted by the EC if
there are no outstanding sums due from the member to
the MU at the time of such application.
12. The name of any person who has been expelled or
has ceased to be a member may be published to the
members and to any other person if considered
expedient.
11

13. Save as required by law, notices to members shall
be deemed to have been published when
communicated via any or all of the following methods:
Statements, messages or notices posted on the MU
website (including via the member’s individual “my MU”
portal) fora minimum of two weeks; direct email via the
email address provided by the member; inclusion in the
MU magazine. Where a member has informed the MU
of individual access requirements, the union will take
such steps as are reasonably practicable so that the
member is not excluded from essential
communications.
Rule XIII: Rates and conditions
1. The EC may for the benefit of members issue general
information concerning the rates and conditions for
different classes of employment and engagement. The
EC shall endeavour to secure that such information
includes any regional variations in rates and conditions
The Applicant’s submissions
13. The application concerns an alleged breach of the rules of the Respondent
Union in respect of the Respondent’s handling of the Applicant’s requests for
legal assistance concerning alleged copyright infringement of the Applicant’s
music. The Applicant submits that, between 2018 and 2026, the Respondent
failed to administer its Legal Assistance Scheme properly; failed to consider
expert forensic musicology evidence; and allowed two officials to operate as
a “Legal Panel” without proper qualifications, independence, minutes,
records, or procedural safeguards. The Applicant also alleges that internal
correspondence disclosed to the Applicant demonstrates bias, hostility,
12

mockery, breach of confidentiality, and concern within the Respondent about
the composition of the body which considered the Applicant’s request. The
application identifies Rule II and Rule XIII as the rules allegedly breached.
The Applicant also refers to later events in 2022 and 2026, which the
Applicant says were linked to the Respondent’s earlier conduct, and asks the
CO to investigate any other breaches that can be identified.
14. Rule II
14.1. In respect of Rule II, the Applicant submits that the Respondent failed
to act consistently with its obligations towards the Applicant as a
member. The Applicant alleges that the Respondent wrongly
questioned or interrupted the Applicant’s membership because the
Applicant lived in Italy, that it refused assistance on the basis that the
Applicant was no longer a member, before later reinstating the
Applicant and changing her professional name without consent. The
Applicant also alleges that the Respondent’s conduct was inconsistent
with protecting the Applicant’s professional interests.
14.2. In respect of jurisdiction, no specific jurisdictional submission is made
which identifies how Rule II, as a membership rule, relates to one of
the matters listed in section 108A(2). The Applicant’s later
jurisdictional submission is directed principally to the body known as
the “Legal Panel” and to the constitution or proceedings of that body,
rather than to the membership provisions in Rule II themselves.
15. Rule XIII
15.1. In respect of Rule XIII, the Applicant submits that the Respondent
breached the rule by failing to properly administer the Legal
Assistance Scheme. The Applicant alleges that the Respondent
allowed two officials to act as a “Legal Panel”; that it ignored the
Applicant’s expert report; that it failed to keep proper records or
13

minutes; that it failed to give reasons; that it relied on subjective views
and informal opinions; and that it allowed hostility and bias to affect
the handling of the Applicant’s request for legal assistance.
15.2. The Applicant emphasised that the complaint is not simply about
disagreement with the outcome of the request for legal assistance, but
that it is about the constitution of the body which considered it and the
procedural bias and alleged malice within that body. In respect of
jurisdiction, the Applicant submits that the “Legal Panel” operated in
substance as an executive committee or decision-making meeting
and that the complaint therefore falls within section 108A(2)(d), as
concerning the constitution or proceedings of such a body. The
Applicant also refers to later events, including alleged consequences
for the Applicant’s health, which the Applicant says were connected
with the Respondent’s earlier handling of the legal assistance issue.
The Jurisdiction of the Certification Officer
16. The CO’s jurisdiction to determine applications for a declaration that a union
has breached its rules is narrow. It is not a general supervisory jurisdiction
over union rule books. Section 108A(1) of the 1992 Act provides that a
member of a trade union may apply to the CO for a declaration that there has
been a breach or threatened breach of the rules of the union relating to:
(a) the appointment or election of a person to, or the removal of a
person from, any office;
(b) disciplinary proceedings by the union (including expulsion);
(c) the balloting of members on any issue other than industrial
action;
14

(d) the constitution or proceedings of any executive committee or of
any decision-making meeting;
(e) such other matters as may be specified in an order made by the
Secretary of State.
17. To fall within this jurisdiction, the application must identify a rule that, properly
construed, relates to a listed matter. The allegations must then be considered
to determine whether, taken at their highest, they engage the rule in that
respect. This is necessary to establish whether the application concerns an
alleged breach of a rule relating to a listed matter within the meaning of
section 108A.
18. On its natural reading, the phrase “relating to” in the context of section 108A
qualifies the rule, not the underlying events or their consequences. The
question is whether the relationship between the rule and one or more of the
listed matters is sufficiently clear and direct for the CO to find that it “relates”.
19. Thus, when addressing jurisdiction, the CO begins by reading the relevant
rule objectively to determine whether, on its face, it relates to one of the listed
matters.
20. Where the rule’s relationship to a listed matter is not immediately clear on its
face, the first question is whether, in its proper operation, the rule has an
inherent aspect that connects it with a listed matter. For this limited purpose,
the CO may consider the facts and circumstances only insofar as they
illuminate the rule’s scope and operation. The facts and circumstances
cannot alter the rule’s meaning or create a relationship the rule does not
inherently bear.
21. Where no such relating aspect is identified, the application will be outside of
the CO’s jurisdiction.
15

22. Where the CO finds that the rule does relate to a listed matter, the CO will
consider whether the allegations, taken at their highest, are capable of
engaging the rule in that relating respect.
23. This recognises that a rule may contain provisions which, in part, relate to a
listed matter, and in part, do not. In such cases, the CO’s jurisdiction will
depend on whether the alleged breach engages the aspect of the rule which
gives it its relationship to the listed matter. Again, the CO may consider the
facts and circumstances of the application for the limited purpose of
understanding whether the alleged breach, taken at its highest, is capable of
engaging the rule in the respect that gives rise to its relationship with a listed
matter. The facts and circumstances cannot convert an unrelated aspect of
a rule into one which relates to a listed matter.
24. Whether in the straightforward or exceptional case, the relationship required
by section 108A must be sufficiently clear and direct and must flow from the
rule itself. Where the only link with a listed matter arises from the events or
consequences of an alleged breach, rather than from the scope or operation
of the rule, the rule cannot be said to “relate” to a listed matter, and the
application will fall outside of the CO’s jurisdiction.
25. In respect of section 108A(2)(d), the jurisdictional requirement has two further
stages.
25.1. Firstly, the rule must relate to an executive committee or decision-
making meeting that meets the definitions found in section 108A
subsections (10) and (11). These definitions are recorded above in the
section of this decision titled “relevant statutory provisions”.
25.2. Secondly, the rule must relate to either the constitution or
proceedings of the relevant committee, as discussed in the following
paragraphs.
16

26. In respect of constitution, the CO has consistently held that this primarily
refers to rules about the composition and structure of those bodies, for
example, membership or quoracy. It can also include rules about when and
how meetings of executive bodies are called, since these affect the proper
functioning of those bodies. However, constitution does not extend to all
constitutional rules of the union, as this would potentially give the CO
jurisdiction over the entire rule book.
27. In respect of proceedings, the CO has consistently held that this primarily
refers to procedural rules governing how business is conducted, rather than
the decisions themselves. Accordingly, jurisdiction is not extended to rules
relating to ‘decision-making’ more broadly, such as rules governing the
substance or merits of decisions. In this context, questions of remit, vires or
‘competent business’ concern whether a qualifying body had authority under
the rules to consider and decide a category of matter, or was required to
proceed by a particular procedure (for example, notice, quorum, voting
method or thresholds); they do not concern whether the outcome was correct
or aligned with the union’s principles, aims or objects.
28. Therefore, although applications about decisions taken during proceedings
are not generally within jurisdiction, the CO may determine an application
where the rule relied upon (a) allocates the subject matter to a particular
qualifying body or withholds it from that body, (b) imposes mandatory
procedural requirements or decision criteria, or (c) limits the options available
and the body chose an option outside those permitted; those are questions
of authority and process, not merits. By contrast, where the rules confer
discretion within the subject matter (for example, to grant or refuse
representation), disagreement with which permitted option was chosen, or a
contention that a different outcome would better reflect the union’s aims or
objects, would typically be better characterised as a complaint about the
merits of the decision, which would not engage section 108A(2)(d), and would
therefore not fall within the jurisdiction of the CO.
17

29. The statutory time limits:
29.1. The 1992 Act contains strict time limits for applications under section
108A. The CO must apply the time limits as prescribed by the Act and
has no discretion to extend them.
29.2. The initial time limit is that an application must be made within six
months of the day on which the breach of rule, or threatened breach
of rule, took place.
29.3. Members are encouraged to use their union’s internal complaints
procedure where one is available. The 1992 Act recognises the
importance of this by extending the time limit for bringing an
application to the CO, where the union’s internal complaints procedure
has been invoked within the initial six-month period, as follows:
i. Where a member invokes the union’s internal complaints
procedure within six months of the alleged breach or threatened
breach, the Act provides a further six-month period in which the
member may apply to the CO. However, the start of that further
six-month period is also fixed by the Act. It does not depend on
any discretion on the part of the CO. The further six-month period
begins with the earlier of two dates:
1. the day on which the unions’ internal complaints procedure
is concluded;
Or,
2. the last day of the one-year period beginning with the day
on which the procedure was invoked.
29.4. In other words, an internal complaints procedure cannot keep time
open indefinitely. For example:
18

i. If an internal complaints procedure is invoked on 1 January and
concludes on 20 January of the same year, the further six-month
period is calculated by reference to 20 January.
ii. If the internal complaints procedure is invoked on 1 January and
has not concluded by 31 December of that year, the further six-
month period is calculated by reference to 31 December, not by
reference to any later date on which the procedure may in fact
conclude.
29.5. For this purpose, invocation of an internal complaints procedure may
be given a fairly wide meaning. However, there must be some
recognisable formal procedure being followed, with identifiable dates
of invocation and conclusion. General correspondence with the union,
informal requests for reconsideration, or continuing disagreement
about the underlying events will not necessarily amount to the
invocation of an internal complaints procedure for the purposes of
section 108A.
29.6. It follows that, when considering time, the CO must identify the date
on which the breach or threatened breach is alleged to have taken
place, and whether any qualifying internal complaints procedure was
invoked within six months of that date. If no qualifying internal
complaints procedure was invoked within that period, time runs from
the date of the alleged breach or threatened breach. If such a
procedure was invoked, time runs in accordance with the statutory
extension described above.
29.7. Where an applicant relies on events spanning a period of time, it is
necessary to distinguish between a later alleged breach, and the
consequences of an earlier alleged breach. The statutory time limit
runs from the date of the alleged breach or threatened breach itself. It
does not run from the date of any later consequence said to flow from
19

that breach, or from the date on which the applicant became aware of
the alleged breach or appreciated its significance.
29.8. The CO has no discretion to extend time because the applicant
became aware of the matter later, or because the applicant says the
consequences of the alleged breach continued or became more
serious at a later date.
Conclusions
30. I must decide whether this application falls within the jurisdiction conferred by
section 108A of the 1992 Act. The application relies on two rules, and such
other rules as the CO may identify. I will assess jurisdiction under section
108A in relation to each rule identified.
31. Rule II
31.1. In respect of Rule II, the rule is concerned with membership. It deals
with eligibility for membership, admission to membership, procedures
for applications, appeals against rejection, regional allocation,
resignation, etc. The rule does not relate to the constitution or
proceedings of an executive committee or decision-making meeting,
nor does it relate to any other listed matter. It concerns membership
administration and the substance of membership decisions, rather
than the composition, structure, quoracy, conduct, or procedure of a
qualifying committee or meeting.
31.2. The Applicant’s allegations about being treated as no longer a
member; being affected by residency in Italy; being reinstated; and
having her professional name changed do not engage Rule II in any
aspect that relates to a matter listed in section 108A(2). Nor is there
material capable of showing that the Respondent’s alleged conduct
under Rule II was taken for a disciplinary purpose. The matters alleged
are, on the Applicant’s own case, about membership administration,
20

service provision, alleged unfairness, and the Respondent’s handling
of the Applicant’s legal assistance request.
31.3. Accordingly, I find that the complaint in respect of Rule II is not within
the jurisdiction of the CO.
31.4. In any event, insofar as the application concerns the Applicant being
treated as no longer a member, the refusal of assistance on that basis,
or the subsequent reinstatement of membership, those matters are
alleged to have occurred in 2020. Insofar as the complaint concerns
the change to the Applicant’s professional name, that is alleged to
have occurred in 2022. The application was made on 23 April 2026.
The Applicant refers to later consequential matters in 2026, and
further correspondence which the Applicant says was directly linked
to the Respondent’s earlier conduct. However, those later matters are
not alleged breaches of Rule II in their own right. They are put forward
as consequences of, or matters connected with, the earlier alleged
conduct. The statutory time limit runs from the date of the alleged
breach or threatened breach of rule itself. It does not run from the date
of any later consequence said to flow from that breach, or from the
date on which the Applicant became aware of the alleged breach or
appreciated its significance. The alleged breach of Rule II is therefore
clearly out of time.
32. Rule XIII
32.1. In respect of Rule XIII, the rule is concerned with rates and conditions.
It provides that the EC may, for the benefit of members, issue general
information concerning the rates and conditions for different classes
of employment and engagement, including regional variations. On its
proper construction, Rule XIII does not contain any provision
governing legal assistance, the composition of a legal panel, the
procedure for considering applications for legal assistance, or the
21

handling of requests for legal support. Taking the Applicant’s case at
its highest, the strongest hypothetical statutory gateway is section
108A(2)(d), because the Applicant submits that a body described as
a “Legal Panel” operated as an executive committee or decision-
making meeting. However, even if I were to agree that the “Legal
Panel” is a qualifying body, Rule XIII itself does not relate to the
constitution or proceedings of the “Legal Panel”.
32.2. The fact that the alleged events may have involved decision-making
by officials, or may have had consequences for the Applicant’s request
for legal assistance, cannot create a relationship between Rule XIII
and the matters listed in section 108A(2). The required relationship
must flow from the rule itself. Rule XIII, on its face and in its proper
operation, relates to information about rates and conditions, not to the
constitution or proceedings of any executive committee or decision-
making meeting, or to any other matter listed in section 108A(2).
32.3. Accordingly, I find that the complaint in respect of Rule XIII is not within
the jurisdiction of the CO.
32.4. In any event, the alleged handling of the Applicant’s request for legal
assistance and the alleged operation of the “Legal Panel” took place
principally in 2019 and 2020, and the Applicant again refers to later
events in 2022 and 2026. However, on the Applicant’s own case,
those later matters are consequences of, or matters connected with,
the alleged earlier handling of the legal assistance process. They are
not later alleged breaches of Rule XIII in their own right. The relevant
date for the statutory time limit is the date of the alleged breach or
threatened breach of rule, not the date of later consequences said to
have flowed from it. On the Applicant’s own case, the alleged breach
of Rule XIII arose from the Respondent’s handling of the legal
assistance process and the alleged composition and conduct of the
22

“Legal Panel” in 2019 and 2020. Therefore, the complaint in respect
of Rule XIII is, again, out of time.
33. Such other rules as the CO may identify
33.1. I have also considered the Applicant’s request that the CO investigate
breaches of any other rules that can be identified by the CO. That is
not a request which the CO has power to grant under section 108A.
The jurisdiction under section 108A is not a general investigatory
jurisdiction over the Respondent’s rule book or conduct. It is for an
applicant to identify the rule or rules said to have been breached and
the breach or threatened breach relied upon. The CO’s role is then to
determine whether that complaint is within the statutory jurisdiction
and, if so, whether the alleged breach is made out. The CO does not
have power under section 108A to investigate at large in order to
identify possible additional breaches which have not been identified
by the Applicant.
33.2. I find that this element of the application is not one which the CO has
jurisdiction to determine.
34. Overall conclusion
34.1. In conclusion, I find that the application, taken at its highest, does not
concern an alleged breach of a rule relating to a matter listed within
section 108A(2) of the 1992 Act. The application concerns the
Respondent’s handling of the Applicant’s requests for legal
assistance, the alleged composition and conduct of the body which
considered those requests, the Respondent’s administration of the
Applicant’s membership and professional name, and later
consequences which the Applicant says flowed from those matters.
Those matters are not within the CO’s jurisdiction unless they engage
23

a rule that relates clearly and directly to one of the listed matters. On
the material provided, they do not.
34.2. Consequently, I find that the application is not one which the CO has
jurisdiction to determine. It cannot therefore be accepted for
determination and is dismissed.
MICHAEL KIDD
The Assistant Certification Officer
19 May 2026
24
description: This document contains the decision made by the Certification Officer in this case.
